title: States of matter — solids, liquids and gases explained by particles
examTip: Remember: during a change of state, the temperature stays CONSTANT. The energy overcomes the forces of attraction between particles. It does not raise their kinetic energy. Examiners love this.
introTips: Think about why steam burns you worse than boiling water. The particle model explains this.
A gas is roughly a thousand times less dense than its solid or liquid. That is because its particles are so spread out.
This topic unlocks pressure, density and latent heat. It is the base for the whole unit.
intro: Why can you squash a gas but not a liquid? Why does ice feel solid while water pours freely? They are the same substance. The answer is in their particles. It depends on how the particles are arranged and how much energy they have. The particle model is one of the most powerful ideas in physics. It explains how all matter behaves using one simple idea. Everything is made of tiny particles that are always moving. Solids, liquids and gases differ in how their particles are arranged. They also differ in how much energy those particles have.

keyPoints.heading: The three states of matter
keyPoints.content: Everything around you is a solid, liquid or gas. The particle model explains why each state behaves as it does. Solid: particles are packed closely together. They sit in a regular pattern called a lattice. They vibrate about fixed positions. They cannot move past each other. There are strong forces of attraction between particles. Solids have a fixed shape and a fixed volume. They are virtually incompressible. Liquid: particles are close together, but not in a regular pattern. They can move past each other freely. The forces between particles are weaker than in a solid. Liquids have a fixed volume. They take the shape of their container. Like solids, they are virtually incompressible. You cannot squeeze the particles any closer together. Gas: particles are far apart. They move quickly in random directions. The forces between particles are negligible, which means almost zero. Gases have no fixed shape or volume. They are highly compressible. There is a lot of empty space between the particles. This space can be squeezed smaller. A change of state changes how particles are arranged and how much energy they have. The particles themselves are NOT created or destroyed.
keyPoints.diagramCaption: Same particles, different arrangement and movement.
writeBullets: Solid — particles in a regular lattice. They vibrate about fixed positions. Strong forces. Fixed shape and volume
Liquid — particles close, but not in a regular pattern. They can move past each other. Weaker forces. Fixed volume
Gas — particles far apart, moving fast in random directions. Negligible forces. No fixed shape or volume
Solids and liquids are virtually incompressible. Gases are highly compressible
A change of state changes how particles are arranged and their energy. Particles are NOT destroyed

keyTerms.def: A regular, repeating arrangement of particles in a solid
Cannot be compressed — volume stays constant under pressure
Attractive forces between particles that hold them together

keyPoints.memTip: SLiG: Solid = Lattice, Liquid = loose, Gas = gone (far apart). Each letter steps up in freedom.
keyPoints.tutor_note: People often say particles in a solid don't move. They DO vibrate. They just can't change position. Get this one right.

keyPoints.heading: Internal energy and the particle model
keyPoints.content: The internal energy of a system is the total kinetic and potential energy of all its particles. The particles are the atoms and molecules that make up the system. It is not the same as temperature. It depends on how many particles there are AND how much energy each one has. When you heat a substance, you increase its internal energy. This can happen in two ways: (a) Temperature rises: particles move faster. Their kinetic energy increases. This is what happens most of the time. (b) Change of state occurs: particles gain potential energy. This happens as the forces of attraction between them are overcome or weakened. The temperature stays CONSTANT, even though energy is still going in. The particle model says: - All matter is made of particles in constant random motion - The higher the temperature, the greater the average kinetic energy of the particles This model explains three things. Gases exert pressure, because particles hit the walls. Diffusion happens, because particles spread out randomly. Substances expand when heated, because particles move faster and push further apart.
writeBullets: Internal energy — the total kinetic and potential energy of ALL the particles in a system
Heating increases internal energy. It either raises temperature OR causes a change of state
Temperature rise — particles gain kinetic energy and move faster
Change of state — particles gain potential energy as forces between particles are overcome. Temperature stays constant
Particle model — all particles are always moving. Higher temperature = greater average kinetic energy

keyTerms.def: The total kinetic and potential energy stored by all particles in a system
Energy due to motion — particles moving faster have more kinetic energy
Energy stored due to the forces of attraction between particles

keyPoints.memTip: Two effects of heating. MOVE faster (kinetic energy ↑) or MOVE apart (potential energy ↑, forces between particles overcome). Temperature only rises for the first one.
keyPoints.tutor_note: The key exam point: temperature stays constant during a change of state. Draw a heating curve. Mark the flat sections clearly.

keyPoints.heading: Changes of state
keyPoints.content: A change of state is when a substance changes from one state to another. All changes of state can be reversed. It is the same substance, just rearranged. Changes of state are physical changes. They differ from chemical changes. If you reverse a change of state, the material gets back its original properties. Mass is conserved in every change of state. This is true for melting, freezing, boiling, evaporating, condensing and sublimating. The particles are the same, so the mass stays the same. Melting (solid → liquid): particles gain energy. The forces between them are partly overcome. Particles begin to move past each other. This happens at the melting point. Freezing (liquid → solid): particles lose potential energy. They arrange themselves into a lattice. This happens at the same temperature as the melting point. Evaporation (liquid → gas): happens at the surface at ANY temperature. Faster-moving particles escape from the surface. This is why wet washing dries even when it is cold. Boiling (liquid → gas): happens all through the liquid at one set temperature, the boiling point. Bubbles of vapour form all through the liquid. Condensation (gas → liquid): particles lose potential energy. Forces pull the particles back together. This happens when a gas cools. Sublimation (solid → gas directly): for example, solid carbon dioxide ('dry ice') sublimates at room temperature. KEY POINT: temperature stays constant during any change of state. The energy is used to overcome the forces of attraction between particles. It is not used to increase kinetic energy.
keyPoints.diagramCaption: The names of each change of state, and which way energy flows.
writeBullets: Melting — solid → liquid. Particles gain energy and break free from their lattice positions
Freezing — liquid → solid. Particles lose energy and form a lattice
Evaporation — liquid → gas at any temperature, from the surface only
Boiling — liquid → gas at the boiling point, all through the liquid
Condensation — gas → liquid. Particles lose energy and forces pull them back together
Sublimation — solid → gas directly (for example, dry ice CO₂)
Changes of state are physical changes. Reverse them and the material gets back its original properties
Mass is conserved in every change of state

keyTerms.def: The temperature at which a substance changes from solid to liquid (same as freezing point)
The specific temperature at which a liquid boils throughout its volume
A change of state directly from solid to gas without passing through liquid

keyPoints.memTip: MFECBS — Melt, Freeze, Evaporate, Condense, Boil, Sublimate. Or think of a heating curve: slope, flat, slope, flat.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Evaporation versus boiling is a common exam question. Make sure you can explain the difference clearly.

keyPoints.heading: Limitations of the particle model
keyPoints.content: The simple particle model treats particles as identical, solid spheres with no features. This is a useful simplification. But it is a model, not reality. What the model gets right: - Explains density differences between states (particles far apart in a gas → low density) - Explains gas pressure (particles hit the container walls) - Explains diffusion (particles move randomly and spread out) - Explains why substances expand when heated (particles move faster and push further apart) - Explains changes of state in words, without numbers Where the model is limited: - Particles are shown as solid spheres - All particles are treated as identical - The model shows no forces between particles At GCSE, the particle model is powerful and it is enough. It correctly predicts and explains a huge range of things in physics. Knowing its limits is an important scientific skill in itself.
writeBullets: The particle model treats particles as identical solid spheres. This is a useful simplification
The model explains density, gas pressure, diffusion, expansion and changes of state
Limitation — particles are shown as solid spheres
Limitation — all particles are treated as identical
Limitation — the model shows no forces between particles
Scientific models are powerful tools, even when they have limits

keyTerms.def: A simplified representation of reality used to explain and predict observations
The spreading out of particles from high to low concentration due to random motion

keyPoints.memTip: All models are wrong, but some are useful. The particle model is very useful at GCSE, even though it is simplified.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Practise explaining what the particle model gets right and where it is limited.

tables.title: Comparing the three states of matter
rows: High (usually a little less than solid)

0.question: Which statement correctly describes particles in a liquid?
options: Particles are close together and can move past each other. This gives a fixed volume but no fixed shape
Particles are in a regular lattice and vibrate about fixed positions
Particles are far apart and move rapidly in random directions
Particles are fixed in position but can vibrate with large amplitude
0.correctFeedback: Exactly right. In a liquid, particles are close together. That gives a fixed volume and makes it virtually incompressible. But they are free to move past each other, so there is no fixed shape.
0.wrongFeedback: Think about the three states. A liquid has a fixed volume, because its particles are still close together. It has no fixed shape, because its particles can flow past each other. The regular lattice is a solid. Far-apart random motion is a gas.

1.question: A substance is being heated at its melting point. What happens to its temperature and internal energy?
options: Temperature stays constant. Internal energy increases, as particles gain potential energy when forces between particles are overcome
Temperature stays constant. Internal energy stays constant
1.correctFeedback: Perfect. During a change of state, temperature is constant. But energy is still going in. It overcomes the forces of attraction between particles, so their potential energy increases. That raises the internal energy.
1.wrongFeedback: Remember: heating always increases internal energy. During a change of state, that extra energy overcomes the forces between particles. It becomes potential energy. It does not speed the particles up, so kinetic energy stays the same. That is why temperature stays constant.

2.question: What is the difference between evaporation and boiling?
options: Evaporation happens at the surface at any temperature. Boiling happens all through the liquid at one set temperature
Evaporation only happens at the boiling point. Boiling can happen at any temperature
Evaporation is a gas turning to liquid. Boiling is a liquid turning to gas
There is no difference. They are the same process
2.correctFeedback: Spot on. Evaporation happens at the surface at any temperature, as faster particles escape. Boiling happens all through the liquid at a fixed boiling point.
2.wrongFeedback: Don't mix these two up. Evaporation: surface only, any temperature. This is why wet clothes dry even when it is cold. Boiling: all through the liquid, only at the boiling point.

3.question: Which of these is a limitation of the simple particle model?
options: It shows all particles as identical solid spheres
It cannot explain why a gas exerts pressure
It cannot explain why gases are less dense than solids
It cannot explain how particles spread out in diffusion
3.correctFeedback: Right. Real particles are not identical solid spheres. The model treats them that way to keep things simple.
3.wrongFeedback: The model does explain gas pressure, density and diffusion. Its limit is how it shows the particles. It treats them all as identical solid spheres.

commonMistakes: Saying particles in a solid 'don't move'. They DO vibrate about fixed positions. They just cannot change their place in the lattice.
Thinking temperature rises during a change of state. It stays constant. The energy is overcoming the forces between particles, not increasing kinetic energy.
Mixing up evaporation and boiling. Evaporation is from the surface at any temperature. Boiling is all through the liquid at the boiling point.
Saying particles are 'destroyed' or 'lost' during a change of state. The same particles are there. They are just rearranged, with different energy.
Mixing up kinetic and potential energy during heating. Temperature change = kinetic energy change. State change = potential energy change.
examTips: If asked what happens to temperature during a change of state, say it stays constant. Explain that the energy overcomes the forces of attraction between particles. Potential energy increases. The particles do not speed up.
When comparing states, always mention four things. Say how particles are arranged and how they move. Mention the forces. Say whether the substance has a fixed shape or volume.
Be clear about evaporation versus boiling. Evaporation: surface, any temperature. Boiling: all through the liquid, fixed boiling point. This comes up often.
revisionCardBullets: Solid: regular lattice, vibrate about fixed positions, strong forces, fixed shape and volume
Liquid: close particles, no regular pattern, can move past each other, fixed volume only
Gas: particles far apart, fast random motion, negligible forces, no fixed shape or volume
Gases are highly compressible. Solids and liquids are virtually incompressible
Internal energy = total kinetic + potential energy of all particles
Heating can raise temperature (kinetic energy ↑) OR cause a change of state (potential energy ↑)
During a change of state: temperature stays CONSTANT
Evaporation: surface only, any temperature. Boiling: all through the liquid, at the boiling point
Melting: forces between particles are overcome, and particles move past each other. Freezing is the reverse
Sublimation: solid → gas directly (for example, dry ice)
Changes of state are physical changes. Mass is conserved in every change of state
Particle model limitations: particles shown as identical solid spheres, with no forces between them
The particle model explains density differences, gas pressure, diffusion and expansion
